newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin mulls power transfer as concern grows.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin mulls power transfer as concern grows.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, in hospital to prepare for heart surgery, on Wednesday considered procedures for handing over power temporarily to his prime minister at talks with his chief of staff.

A Kremlin statement issued after the talks with chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais made clear Yeltsin would name Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to deputise for him and control the "nuclear button" while he has heart surgery.
The statement was the clearest signal so far that Yeltsin intends to go ahead with a brief transfer of his duties, including control of Russia's nuclear missiles, but gave no details of his plans.

"Several questions on the mechanisms for transferring power, including control of the so-called 'nuclear button', to the chairman of the Russian government (prime minister) during the president's planned operation, were also discussed," the presidential press service statement said.

Brief Russian television extracts of the 40-minute meeting with Chubais at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital showed the 65-year-old president in a white open-necked shirt and cardigan shaking hands and then moving freely as he took his seat.
Yeltsin said he was largely satisfied with cooperation in Moscow over peace moves in rebel Chechnya and the two men discussed regional elections and the planned 1997 budget.

Despite Yeltsin's good appearance, concern over his health has been heightened by the extension of his stay in hospital until the end of this week. He had been expected to leave the hospital last Sunday after going in for checks last Friday.
"There is no good news about the president's health," Ekho Moskvy radio station said in a commentary.
Ekho Moskvy dismissed a suggestion by presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky that Yeltsin had demonstrated his fitness by meeting Chernomyrdin for about an hour on Tuesday.
It said Russia's problems were too big for the two men to cover them properly in just an hour.
Doctors are due to meet on September 25 or 26 to decide when Yeltsin should have a bypass operation to improve the flow of blood to his heart.
Chubais said in an interview published on Wednesday that he expected the president to hand over his duties to Chernomyrdin by decree for a period of 10 hours to a maximum of two days.
"As for the key questions, despite his illness the president is not only in touch but is taking decisions," Chubais told the newspaper Izvestia.
But the interview, published on Wednesday, was conducted with the newspaper on Friday evening, before doctors decided to extend the president's hospital stay.
Chubais said Chernomyrdin and other officials were already taking some decisions which were previously taken by Yeltsin.
Speculation is growing that Yeltsin's extended stay in hospital was prompted by concern that his overall state of health is not good enough for him to have major heart surgery.
"It seems the doctors do not want to operate on him because of his general physical condition," a source in the opposition Communist Party told Reuters.
Yeltsin has said he would be able to work only in a passive way if he did not have surgery. This could put the nature of the presidency in question and have huge political implications.
The Kremlin has denied there are any complications in Yeltsin's condition, despite persistent rumours that his liver has been damaged by drink or that he has other health problems.
But the Kremlin's newly declared policy of openness has left unanswered many questions about Yeltsin's condition and the operation he is due to have.
